content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors tackle the problem of open-set image recognition. They build their method on top of a very well-established vision-language pre-trained model, CLIP. They propose to divide the training dataset into small mutually exclusive groups. Then they learn the prompt specific to each group. To mitigate the label bias of pre-trained CLIP, they propose negative label words sampled from WordNet. For testing, they aggregate individual group predictions by a simple maximum operation to get the final prediction. They validate the proposed method on public open-set recognition benchmarks: CIFAR10, CIFAR100, LSUN, and ImageNet. The claimed contributions are as follows:

C1. They propose a new paradigm for open-set recognition: group-guided prompt engineering.

C2. To mitigate the label bias of pre-trained CLIP, they propose to use open negative label during contrastive learning in each group training.

C3. They propose group combined testing, which is a simple maximum operation across different groups’ top-1 predictions.

C4. They conduct extensive experiments to validate the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper has the following strengths.

S1. The problem they tackle, open-set image recognition is important and interesting. To deploy image recognition models, the models should be able to detect unknown classes as we cannot train the models with all the classes in the world. 

S2. The simple method they propose works quite well across many datasets. Unknown detection performance on CIFAR and ImageNet is favorable compared to the existing methods as shown in Tables 1 and 2.

S3. The grouping mechanism seems to be effective in separating known distributions from unknown distributions as shown in Figure 3.

However, this paper has a few weaknesses as well.

W1. Insufficient validation.
There are unvalidated claims they make in the paper. 

1) How do we guarantee the open negative labels sampled from WordNet are irrelevant to downstream tasks? There is no information on how to sample open negative labels from WordNet. 
2) The individual contribution of grouping and open negative labels is unknown. Although the gain from the proposed method is quite significant, we do not know where the gain comes from. What is the performance if we do not use open negative labels?

W2. Poor presentation quality. 
First of all, Figure numbers and Table numbers are wrong many times. For example, In section 4.2, the authors refer to Table 8 in the Appendix instead of Table 1 in the main paper. In section 4.4, they refer to Table 8 in the Appendix and Table 2 which seems irrelevant. In section 4.6 they refer to Figure 8 in the Appendix instead of Figure 3 in the main paper. In section 4.7 last paragraph, they refer to Table 4 which seems irrelevant. In addition, there are many typos and awkward, and wrong sentences throughout the paper. To list a few:

1) “Considering the sum of probabilities on group-specific closed-set classes to be the score of being known.” -> Not an English sentence.

2) “It validates tha the proposed method mitigates….” -> typo

I have a few clarification questions for the authors.

Q1. In eq (7), S_{open} is defined. However, we predict known labels or unknown with eq (8) anyway. Where do we use S_{open}? Why not unify eq(7) and (8)?

Q2. Why divide the small datasets by their names in order (alphabetical order probably)? What if we use WNID order in this case as well?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As far as I know this work is the first to divide training data into groups to tackle the open-set recognition problem. The improvement from the proposed method seems quite significant, although individual contribution from each component is unvalidated. There are a few uncertain points due to the presentation quality as I mention above. Therefore, I think it is novel and has a good quality of experimental results. However, it requires additional experimental results to further validate the claims they make and requires some amount of rewriting.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think this paper has its merit. However, it requires some clarifications, further validation experiments to be published.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a divide-and-conquer strategy for open-set recognition tasks by dividing the closed-set data into one or more groups (a tuned hyperparameter). The proposed group-specific contrastive tuning (GCTu) leverages the open negative label words from WordNet (Miller, 1995) for better regularization. The proposed group combined testing (GCTe) determines the optimal prediction prompt by focusing on the group-wise closed-set probability distribution. Comparable results are achieved on ImageNet and other smaller-scale datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The finding of prompt bias itself is non-trivial. Most of the recent prompt engineering works do not discuss this important issue but simply throwing lots of engineering design to the pipeline. The prompt bias analysis for open-set recognition tasks is appreciated.
- Various figures (Fig 1 & Fig 2) are helpful in comprehending the proposed GCTu and GCTe components.
- The idea of using WordNet to compensate for open-set biases is straightforward and natural.
- Experiments on both small and large benchmarks is a plus.

Weaknesses
- It’s not clear whether the claims of the proposed group combined testing (GCTe) components are technically correct. Eq.6 chooses the optimal prompt from the group that has the highest probability value. However, different groups are not directly comparable due to different numbers of training samples from different datasets (e.g. small vs large scale datasets). Also, when the model is trained on datasets with class imbalanced distributions, classes with more training samples receive more gradient updates, usually ending up with higher probability value during inference. Therefore, it is not well justified whether the GCTe component works as described in the manuscript.
- Following above, if the proposed GCTe component works well, why do we need an extra hyper-parameter Tau in Eq.8. How sensitive is this threshold tau? What would happen if we removed this threshold in practice?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The novelty and reproducibility are good. Clarity can be improved, especially for Sec 3.3 on the group combined testing (GCTe) component.
content.summary_of_the_review: The submission brought new insight into prompt biases for open-set recognition tasks. I would appreciate more clarity on Sec 3.3 as mentioned in the weaknesses.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an open-set recognition method on large-scale datasets based on pre-trained vision-language model. It engages language prompt learning into getting better language prompts for OSR problem in downstream datasets. To solve this problem, a tuning method with open negative label words introduced is proposed. Furthermore, grouping strategy is adopted for tuning those learnable tokens to form the language prompts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- Strength
    1. How to utilize CLIP to solve large scale OSR problem is worth exploring and the newly proposed paradigm is interesting. 
    2. The performance gains a lot when compared to the baseline which uses CLIP for close-set recognition and detects out-of-distribution samples.
- Weaknesses
    1. The overall novelty of the paper is limited. Although a new paradigm is proposed, the methods are built upon the existing prompt-based language models and the technical contribution is limited. 
    2. The grouping strategy aims to avoid learning shared context tokens for all classes. However, why this strategy benefits open-set recognition is not well motivated.
    3. The introduced open negative label words are selected from WordNet which also covers the label words of ImageNet. In this way, the proposed open negative label pool might carry a lot of prior knowledge and cause a good result in large-scale experiments. However, when this method is used in real open-set scenarios, it might fail because no information on open-set classes is accessible. When the tested open-set class is similar to one of the closed-set classes and has no relation to selected open negative words, it will still be detected as a closed-set class. It is proper to give the selected open negative words and unknown open-set classes in experiments.
    4. Several experiments show that grouping is a helpful strategy for language prompt learning but it still lacks the illustration about why we should group by WNID order. This might also verify that too much prior knowledge is introduced in the open negative label pool, which violates the realistic open-set setting.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well presented. However, the novelty is limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, the overall novelty of the paper is limited. Moreover, the knowledge introduced for dealing with open-set recognition may violate the realistic open-set settings. For example, how to select open negative label words is the key to the success of improving OSR results, while the paper fails to explain the selection strategy, which requires further clarifications.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper tackles the problem of open-set recognition, a problem in which models are trained on a finite set of categories before being tasked with detecting images from new categories as ‘unseen’ at test-time. In particular, the paper tackles the problem through the lens of prompt tuning, a parameter efficient way for fine-tuning large-scale vision-language models (like CLIP) for a downstream classification task. 

The authors propose to split the training categories into G disjoint groups and learn an independent prompt for each one (the method is termed GCTu). At test-time, independent classifications are performed within each group, and the group with the maximum softmax probability is selected. The sum over softmax probabilities in this group is taken as the open-set score (the method is termed GCTe). Furthermore, the authors propose to collect a set of WordNet concepts which do not occur in the training set and treat these as a negative concept set during training, by passing the nouns as distractor concepts to the text encoder.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
* The idea of using WordNet concepts as ‘negatives’ is interesting. It is usually difficult to collect ‘negative’ images when training open-set image classifiers; for instance, it has been shown that Outlier Exposure is highly sensitive to the choice of outlier dataset. On the other hand, negative concepts in text seems to be easier to mine, and the authors show in an ablation that this helps. 
* The authors report strong results for the task of open-set recognition, outperforming some baselines. 

Weaknesses:
* The authors use a CLIP backbone (trained on 400M image-text pairs) and compare this in their main tables to models trained from scratch on small datasets, mostly without comment. The authors highlight that ZOC also adapts a CLIP backbone but do not adequately discuss the fact that CLIP has likely ‘seen’ many of the open-set concepts during training. 
* When discussing Table 2, the authors also discuss that the CLIP training set has been filtered of any ImageNet images. However, this also obfuscates the point that images from the same *categories* as the open-set examples have likely been encountered.
* The authors run a zero-shot classification + MSP baseline. While I acknowledge the authors’ effort in including a baseline, I do not think it is a fair comparison, as the model has never explicitly been trained for classification on the closed-set classes. A fairer, simple, baseline would be to fine-tune CLIP for closed-set classification, and running MSP on top of this. 
* On a similar note, the authors run an ablation on the number of groups which gives best performance, finding that on standard (albeit small-scale) benchmarks, one group works best. This is very close to doing standard prompt tuning on the closed-set, and running MSP on top of this. The authors could include this as a baseline. 
* The authors mention that their goal is not to achieve SoTA. However, they should for clarity mention methods which report stronger performance on the standard benchmarks. For instance [1] reports stronger performance on some benchmarks while training their model from scratch on the closed-set. 
* The authors claim that open-set performance falls when models are trained on ImageNet, and that weak backbone models fail on this task. [2] shows that open-set performance on ImageNet can, in fact, be improved substantially by simply taking models with higher closed-set accuracy. The paper does this by experimenting with stronger and larger backbones (e.g EfficientNet-B7) 
* The authors could cite the closed-set accuracy of all models they compare to. This would help control for the strength of the backbone they use in their method.
* Finally, the authors claim a main motivation behind this work is to develop a method which can uniformly be applied to large and small-scale datasets. I find this confusing, as I think most OSR methods can equally well be applied to large and small datasets (e.g OpenMax, MSP, MLS) and only a few may struggle with scale (e.g those using generative models like OSRCI or OpenGAN [1]). In fact, I would suggest that the authors conclusion that grouping is not beneficial on small-scale datasets actually means the proposed method is not uniformly suitable across large and small datasets.

[1] OpenGAN, Kong and Ramanan, ICCV ’21
[2] Open-set Recognition: a Good Closed-set Classifier is All You Need? Vaze et al, ICLR 22
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity of writing in this paper is medium. At times, I felt that the mathematical notations obfuscated a simple idea which could be communicated in text. For instance, when describing the way groups are constructed, it seems to me that G equally sized groups are created of N_max size. The final group is smaller if the total number of categories is not divisible by N_max. In my opinion, this is easier to understand than Eq 1.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper could be interesting in that the authors explore open-set recognition in the context of a large-scale CLIP model. However, the comparisons in the paper are not made under a fair setting, and the use of large-scale pre-training for detecting 'unseen' categories should be very carefully argued, with all caveats clearly specified. Furthermore, I cannot be convinced of the methods' efficacy without some baselines as I suggested above (which I suggest are simple and intuitive).
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
